questions.q: What is the purpose of the `name` attribute on an `<input>` element, and what happens if you omit it?
questions.a: The `name` attribute is the key under which the input's value is sent to the server during form submission. If omitted, that input's data is **not included** in the form data payload at all — the server receives nothing for that field. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's for CSS styling" or "it's the label text") reveals the student confuses `name` with `id` (used for labeling/JS) or `placeholder` (UI hint), and doesn't understand the client-server data contract.

questions.q: Explain the difference between `<label for="email">Email:</label> <input type="email" id="email">` and `<label>Email: <input type="email"></label>`. Which is better for accessibility and why?
questions.a: Both associate the label with the input, but the first (explicit) uses `for`/`id` matching while the second (implicit) wraps the input inside the label. The explicit method is **better for accessibility** because some screen readers and older assistive technologies only reliably announce labels linked via `for`/`id`; wrapping can fail in complex layouts (e.g., when input is inside a different container). A wrong answer claiming "they're identical" or "wrapping is better because less code" shows the student hasn't tested with assistive tech and misses the robustness requirement in WCAG.

questions.q: A form has `method="get"` and `action="/search"`. The user enters "informatics practices" in a text input named `q` and clicks submit. Write the exact URL the browser navigates to, and explain why spaces become `+` or `%20`.
questions.a: The browser navigates to `/search?q=informatics+practices` (or `%20` instead of `+`). With `method="get"`, form data is appended to the `action` URL as a query string: `?` followed by `name=value` pairs separated by `&`. Spaces are not allowed in URLs, so they are percent-encoded: `+` (application/x-www-form-urlencoded legacy) or `%20` (RFC 3986 standard). A wrong answer like `/search q=informatics practices` (no `?`, no encoding) reveals the student doesn't understand HTTP GET request structure or URL encoding rules.

questions.q: Compare `type="radio"` and `type="checkbox"` for a "Select your course" field where the user must choose exactly one of: Science, Commerce, Humanities. Which input type is correct, and what HTML attribute **must** be identical across all options to enforce single selection?
questions.a: Use `type="radio"` — radio buttons enforce **mutually exclusive** selection (only one in a group can be checked). The `name` attribute **must be identical** (e.g., `name="course"`) for all three radio inputs; this groups them so the browser deselects the previous when a new one is chosen. Using `checkbox` would allow multiple selections (wrong for "exactly one"), and using different `name` values would break the grouping (all could be checked simultaneously). A wrong answer choosing `checkbox` or suggesting `id` groups them shows confusion between grouping mechanism (`name`) and unique identification (`id`).

questions.q: A student writes a file upload form: `<form action="/upload" method="post"> <input type="file" name="photo"> <button type="submit">Upload</button> </form>`. The file never reaches the server. Identify the missing form attribute, explain why it's required, and state the exact value it must have.
questions.a: Missing: `enctype="multipart/form-data"` on the `<form>`. Default encoding (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) cannot transmit binary file data — it only handles text key-value pairs. `multipart/form-data` splits the request body into MIME parts, each with its own headers (Content-Disposition, Content-Type), allowing binary files to be sent intact. Without it, the server receives an empty or corrupted file field. A wrong answer suggesting `method="get"` (files **cannot** be uploaded via GET) or `enctype="text/plain"` (not standard for files) reveals the student doesn't understand HTTP request body encoding mechanisms.

questions.q: Design a minimal but complete HTML form for a "Library Book Suggestion" feature. Requirements: (1) Book title (required text), (2) Author (required text), (3) Genre (dropdown: Fiction, Non-Fiction, Science, History, Other), (4) Your name (optional text), (5) Anonymous checkbox (if checked, hide name field via HTML only — no JS), (6) Submit button. Write the full HTML. Explain how you'd handle the "anonymous hides name" requirement **without JavaScript**.
questions.a:
**HTML:**
```html
<form action="/suggest" method="post">
  <label for="title">Book Title *</label>
  <input type="text" id="title" name="title" required>

  <label for="author">Author *</label>
  <input type="text" id="author" name="author" required>

  <label for="genre">Genre *</label>
  <select id="genre" name="genre" required>
    <option value="">Select...</option>
    <option value="fiction">Fiction</option>
    <option value="non-fiction">Non-Fiction</option>
    <option value="science">Science</option>
    <option value="history">History</option>
    <option value="other">Other</option>
  </select>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Your Details</legend>
    <label for="anonymous">Post anonymously</label>
    <input type="checkbox" id="anonymous" name="anonymous" value="1">

    <label for="name">Your Name</label>
    <input type="text" id="name" name="name">
  </fieldset>

  <button type="submit">Suggest</button>
</form>
```
**No-JS "anonymous hides name":** Pure HTML/CSS cannot *conditionally hide* a field based on checkbox state — that requires JavaScript (covered in c12_ip_cbse_06_011/012). The correct answer: **"This cannot be done with HTML alone; you need JavaScript to toggle `hidden` or `display: none` on the name field when the checkbox changes. In HTML-only, you'd either (a) always show name but make it optional, or (b) use two separate forms/pages."** A student who claims `required` on name + checkbox logic works in HTML reveals they confuse client-side validation with dynamic DOM manipulation.
